idiom_name: protocols with associated types + protocol extensions + conditional conformance
implementation_notes: Swift's protocols plus extensions are the local form of the descriptor: a protocol declares the properties (associatedtype, static requirements), a conformance binds them for a type - retroactively too, from your own module, for a type you do not own - and a protocol extension supplies the behaviour that follows from the property, with where-constrained extensions behaving like partial specializations and the most specialized matching extension winning. Conditional conformance (extension Array: Equatable where Element: Equatable) derives a property from a type parameter's properties, the exact analogue of a descriptor computed from the described type, and the standard library's numeric protocols (AdditiveArithmetic, Numeric, Comparable) form the trait hierarchy for arithmetic. A detached descriptor is needed only when the description must live outside the type (a codec/format table keyed by ObjectIdentifier or metatype).
pitfalls: A protocol with an associated type is not a first-class type: any Described erases the payload, so generic code must stay generic (some Described / a type parameter) or the associated value becomes unusable inside the body.

Methods that are not protocol requirements live only in the protocol extension, and calls made through the protocol type use the extension's implementation even when the concrete type declares a same-named method - non-requirement members are not dynamically dispatched, which silently selects the wrong behaviour.

Retroactive conformances (an imported type to an imported protocol) conflict with another module doing the same and are diagnosed when both load; prefer defining your own protocol or wrapping the type.
